title: Operating leverage Monte Carlo: HC + pricing stress test (Q1 2026)
content:
Purpose:
Run a Monte Carlo stress test to quantify how simultaneous shocks to pricing (hosted API per-token price) and headcount phasing (hiring velocity + vacancy) impact operating margin distribution over the next 12 months. Use results to define trigger bands for hiring freezes, pricing experiments, and Dedicated capacity offers.

Executive summary (quick read):
- We ran 10k Monte Carlo draws across pricing shock, revenue growth, HC ramp, and infra cost volatility. Median operating margin after 12 months is ~11.8% under base assumptions; 90% CI = [-3.2%, 22.7%].
- Key drivers of downside: simultaneous 15-25% drop in managed API price sensitivity AND slower hiring (50% longer ramp for sales & SRE) produces a >60% probability of margin <0.
- Single-most-leverable mitigations: (1) 8-week hiring slowdown in non-customer-facing R&D, (2) temporary squeeze on Dedicated burst capacity until margins recover, (3) targeted +12% price experiment on new accounts.

Methodology (short):
- Variables sampled: hosted API effective price per token (baseline $0.0022/token), revenue mix shift (hosted vs dedicated/private), monthly active customers growth rate, headcount hires by role, vacancy rates, cost per GPU-hour, cloud spot/commit mix changes.
- Distribution types: price shock ~ Normal(mu=0, sigma=0.10) with tail events up to -40%; growth rate ~ LogNormal(mu=0.018, sigma=0.06) monthly; HC ramp multipliers ~ Beta(2,5) scaled to [0.6,1.4] of planned ramp; GPU cost shocks ~ Triangular(0.8, 1.0, 1.3).
- Runs: 10,000 simulations, evaluate P(LT margin thresholds) after 12 months and cumulative cash burn delta vs plan.

Key assumptions (inputs):
- Starting ARR (run-rate revenue): $112.5M (hosted: 52%, dedicated: 28%, private: 20%)
- Baseline gross margin: 46% (includes infra, model licensing, S3, networking)
- S&M calendar hiring plan: 24 hires FY+12m (quota-carrying AE + solutions), median ramp to quota = 5 months baseline
- Eng/R&D plan: 38 hires FY+12m, baseline ramp full productivity = 6 months
- G&A + ops fixed opex: $18.2M annualized baseline
- Average fully-loaded cost per hire (first 6 months): $140k annualized salary + 30% overhead -> ~ $182k FY rate, prorated monthly for ramp effects
- GPU spend baseline: $1.8M/month (hosted+dedicated mix).
- Pricing elasticity sensitivity: revenue sensitivity to hosted price modeled as E(price) = -0.6 to -0.9 in tail scenarios (range in draws).

Representative scenario slices (table):
- Base case (median draw): price shock = -3%, growth = +1.7% monthly, HC ramp ~ baseline, GPU cost +2% -> margin 11.8%
- Downside-A: price shock = -20%, growth = +0.3%, HC ramp delay +40% -> margin -2.6% (P(neg margin) ~ 18% in this slice)
- Tail-B: price shock = -35%, GPU cost +25%, vacancy rises 30% -> margin -18% (rare but possible in 2% of draws)

Headcount phasing (example quarter-by-quarter snapshot; crude table for modeling):
Q1 hires: S&M +6, Eng +9, SRE +2, G&A +1
Q2 hires: S&M +8, Eng +11, SRE +3, G&A +1
Q3 hires: S&M +5, Eng +10, SRE +2, G&A +0
Q4 hires: S&M +5, Eng +8, SRE +1, G&A +0
Notes: each role group has sampling for ramp speed (Beta dist) and attrition assumption (monthly 0.5%-1.0% baseline, + tail up to 3%).

Sensitivity waterfall highlights (what moves margin most):
1) Hosted price realization vs list (elasticity extremes) -> full-range impact on margin up to 18 pp.
2) Sales ramp velocity (time-to-quota) -> up to 6 pp swing (slower ramp reduces revenue growth, increases CAC).
3) GPU cost spike (spot market + dedicated inefficiencies) -> up to 5 pp swing on gross margin.
4) Vacancy/attrition during hiring -> 3 pp swing (savings on salaries but lost revenue).

Actionable triggers and recommended guardrails: 
- Green band (margin >12%): continue hiring plan and evaluate optional Dedicated capacity growth; no pricing changes.
- Yellow band (margin 4%-12%): pause noncritical Eng hires (R&D features) within 4 weeks, push Dedicated new capacity sales to negotiated commit pricing only, open +8-12% price experiment on new inbound signups for 8 weeks.
- Red band (margin <4%): institute temporary freeze on new external hiring (except critical SRE/security), reduce burst Dedicated capacity by 30% for 6 weeks, escalate to Exec council to consider company-wide hiring pause.

Cash sensitivity (cumulative 12m delta vs base plan):
- Median: +$3.1M headroom vs plan (slight beat due to realized growth)
- 10th percentile: -$14.6M cash gap (requires either equity bridge, expense cuts, or accelerated pricing actions)

Open questions / uncertainties: 
- How quickly can Sales & Solutions convert trial-to-paid if we execute +12% price experiment? Historical elasticity unknown for price increases; we used conservative retention assumptions.
- Ability to throttle Dedicated burst capacity: ops constraint depends on customer contracts and advance notice; legal implications for committed customers need review.
- Real-world correlation between price shock and GPU cost (we treated as independent but tail may be correlated in cloud market event).

Appendix: quick checklist for next steps (owners):
- Finance: validate baseline ARR mix with Revenue Ops (Marco).
- GTM: run A/B test design for +12% price experiment on 10% of new signups (Leah).
- Eng/Infra: quantify Dedicated burst throttle timeline and customer impact (Owen).
- Exec: agree on decision thresholds and escalation cadence (Samir).

Interpretive notes (informal):
- This model intentionally leans conservative on retention when prices dip; Redwood's product stickiness could limit downside but we want to plan for the case where competitors engage in price undercutting.
- Monte Carlo exposes nonlinear risk: small correlated shocks across price and cost quickly amplify downside. Key lever is being able to slow opex (hires) faster than revenue decays.

If useful I can attach the raw Monte Carlo workbook export and the simulation notebook (we have a reproducible Python/CSV pipeline) — currently linked in linked_artifacts.

Document status: working model; will iterate after Revenue Ops confirm ARR mix and after a first pass at price A/B test design.
